drivingQuestion: Does a bill of divorce thrown into her bed in his house divorce her, given the dispute over a buyer's vessels in the seller's domain?
outcomeNote: The difficulty is answered in the next unit (gittin.sugya323).

segments.he: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: בְּמִטָּה שֶׁלּוֹ – אֵינָהּ מְגוֹרֶשֶׁת, בְּמִטָּה שֶׁלָּהּ – מְגוֹרֶשֶׁת.
segments.en: «This is also taught» in a baraita: «Rabbi Eliezer says:» If he throws the bill of divorce to her when she is «in his bed, she is not divorced;» if he throws it to her when she is «in her bed, she is divorced.»

segments.he: וּבְמִטָּה שֶׁלָּהּ – מְגוֹרֶשֶׁת? כִּלְיוֹ שֶׁל לוֹקֵחַ בִּרְשׁוּת מוֹכֵר הוּא; שָׁמְעַתְּ מִינַּהּ: כִּלְיוֹ שֶׁל לוֹקֵחַ בִּרְשׁוּת מוֹכֵר – קָנָה לוֹקֵחַ?
segments.en: The Gemara asks: And if he throws the bill of divorce to her «in her bed, is she divorced?» But the bed «is» like «vessels of a buyer» that are «in the domain of the seller,» since the bed that belongs to her is in the house of the husband. Can «you conclude from» here that even if the «vessels of a buyer» are «in the domain of the seller, the buyer acquires» anything that is deposited into his vessels? This issue is disputed elsewhere. Some hold that when a vessel of the buyer is in the domain of the seller, the vessel cannot serve to acquire an item on behalf of the buyer.
